sequences.title: The Mali Empire: Gold, Salt & the City of Books

screens.title: A kingdom built on… salt?
lines: Salt seems boring — it sits on every table. But your body can't live without it, and in the blazing lands south of the Sahara it was desperately hard to get.
Medieval West Africa had something else in absurd supply: gold. Two treasures, two homelands, and a desert in between — that's a recipe for an empire.

vocab.meaning: a group of merchants and camels crossing the desert together
a West African storyteller-musician who keeps history alive by memory
the Mande word for emperor

sequences.title: India: The Power of Zero & the Winds of Trade

screens.title: The most powerful number is nothing
lines: Write 507. That zero looks like it's doing nothing — but delete it and the number collapses to 57.
The system you do ALL your math in — ten digits, place value, zero — was worked out by mathematicians in India during the Gupta 'golden age.' Today you meet them.

vocab.meaning: a written symbol for a number, like 7 or VII
a stretch of peace and wealth when art and science bloom

screens.title: Winds you can set a calendar by
lines: Each summer, ocean winds sweep INTO India loaded with rain; each winter they reverse and blow dry air out to sea.
Sailors learned to ride this giant schedule like a free conveyor belt — out one season, home the next.

vocab.meaning: a seasonal wind that reverses direction twice a year

sequences.title: China: Four Inventions & the Treasure Fleet

screens.title: Made in China (a thousand years early)
lines: Paper. Printed books. The compass. Fireworks. One civilization invented all four — centuries before anyone else had them.
Tang and Song China was the tech giant of the medieval world. Let's open the workshop.

vocab.meaning: one family's line of rulers, like the Tang or the Song
super-hard, glass-smooth pottery fired blazing hot
an early chemist hunting for magical potions

screens.title: The hardest test in the world
lines: How do you pick the people who run an empire — by birth, or by brains?
Song China's answer was a famously brutal civil-service exam. Pass it, and a farmer's son could become a governor.

vocab.meaning: the officials who run a government's daily work
earning a place by skill, not by birth

sequences.title: Medieval Europe: Castles, Guilds & the Great Sickness

screens.title: The land-for-loyalty deal
lines: No police, no salaries, no big governments — so how did medieval Europe organize itself? With a giant chain of promises.
Kings granted land to lords, lords pledged knights to kings, and peasants worked the fields in exchange for protection. That chain is called feudalism.

vocab.meaning: the medieval system of trading land for loyalty and protection
a noble who receives land from a lord in exchange for service
a peasant bound to a manor's land, not free to leave without permission

screens.title: Reading a castle like a blueprint
lines: A castle is a machine for defense — every odd detail has a job.
Ring of water, lifting bridge, crashing iron gate: learn the parts and you can 'read' any castle, even the ones in your favorite wizard books.

vocab.meaning: the water-filled ditch ringing a castle
a bridge that lifts to seal the castle entrance
the heavy iron grate that drops to block the gate

screens.title: From one copy a year to hundreds a month
lines: Remember the monks hand-copying books, one slow year per Bible? Around 1440 a German goldsmith named Gutenberg built a machine that shattered that bottleneck.
When copying gets cheap, ideas spread like wildfire — and Europe caught fire with new art and science. 'Renaissance' means rebirth.

vocab.meaning: a machine that stamps inked type onto paper, hundreds of copies at a time
reusable metal letters you rearrange to print any page
a wealthy supporter who pays artists or scientists to work

screens.title: Don't argue — look!
lines: For centuries, hard questions about nature were settled by quoting ancient books. The Scientific Revolution flipped the habit: a claim needs EVIDENCE anyone can check.
You already do this in science class — claim, evidence, reasoning. Now meet the man who aimed a telescope at Jupiter and let the sky testify.

vocab.meaning: observations that back up or sink a claim
a tube of lenses that makes far things look near

screens.title: Why risk the open ocean?
lines: In 1450s Europe, pepper and nutmeg were worth fortunes — every sack passed through a dozen middlemen, and every middleman charged a markup.
Sailors who could reach the source by SEA would skip them all. New ships and borrowed tools made them dare to try.

vocab.meaning: a small, nimble ship whose triangular sails could angle into the wind
a tool that measures a star's height to find how far north or south you are
the art of knowing where you are and steering where you mean to go

screens.title: The great food swap
lines: Until 1492, the two halves of the planet swapped almost nothing: no tomatoes in Italy, no potatoes in Ireland, no horses anywhere in the Americas.
Columbus's voyages reconnected the halves, and everything crossed: foods, animals — and, tragically, germs. Historians call it the Columbian Exchange.

vocab.meaning: the global swap of plants, animals, and diseases that followed 1492
your body's trained defense against a disease it has met before

items.prompt: Why would anyone trade gold for salt — sometimes weight for weight? Let's follow the caravans.

steps.text: In Mali's southern lands, gold was astonishingly common — the mansa could pile it up. But the region had almost no salt, and in fierce heat, bodies lose salt fast and food spoils without it.

Deep in the Sahara sat Taghaza, a town that mined slabs of salt. The traveler Ibn Battuta visited and found even its houses built of salt blocks. So: the desert had salt, the south had gold — each side craved the other's treasure.

check.question: Why was salt worth a fortune in Mali's gold country?
options: Salt was scarce there, but bodies and food storage demanded it
Salt was heavier than gold
The gold mines had run out

steps.text: Camel caravans shuttled between the two worlds: salt slabs south, gold north. Value comes from scarcity — in some markets, a pound of salt really could trade for a pound of gold.
Mali grew rich by sitting in the middle: every load that crossed its territory paid a tax to the mansa. Control the crossroads, collect the wealth.

check.question: How did Mali profit without mining either treasure itself?
options: By taxing every caravan that crossed its territory
By keeping all the salt for the royal kitchens
By selling camels to both sides

items.prompt: A trade-caravan cat named Sahel rides the route. Complete her cargo log.

lines: Salt slabs from the desert mines travel [[south]] to the Niger River markets
Gold from the southern lands travels [[north]] toward the Mediterranean coast
Either way, every camel-load pays a tax to the [[mansa|emperor]]

items.hint: Picture the map: desert (and its salt mines) to the north, gold country to the south, Mali between.
items.explanation: Salt south, gold north — and Mali, ruling the crossroads, taxed both directions into a fortune.

items.prompt: Who founded the Mali Empire around 1235 — a hero still celebrated in an epic performed today?
options: Sundiata
Mansa Musa
Ibn Battuta
Askia the Great
items.hint: Griots call him the Lion King of Mali.
items.explanation: Sundiata united the region after the Battle of Kirina, and griots have performed the Epic of Sundiata for nearly 800 years.

items.prompt: What made the camel the 'ship of the desert' for Sahara crossings?
items.answer: It can march for days without drinking, then gulp around 100 liters at once
options: It can march for days without drinking, then gulp around 100 liters at once
It can outrun a horse over any distance
It can smell water buried under the sand
It never needs to sleep
items.hint: Think water.
items.explanation: Camels can go days between drinks, then swallow roughly a bathtub's worth in minutes — perfect for a crossing that took about two months.

items.prompt: Mali's official historians carried no books — they performed centuries of history from memory, with music.

lines: These living libraries of West Africa are called [[griots|griot]]

items.hint: The bridge introduced this word — it starts with g.
items.explanation: Griots passed the Epic of Sundiata down by voice for centuries — and griot families still perform across West Africa today.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Saharan caravans — tap the lie.

truths: Large caravans could number in the thousands of camels
Crossing the Sahara took around two months
data.lie: Camels store water in their humps for the journey

items.hint: One of these is a famous animal myth.
items.explanation: Humps store FAT, not water — an energy pantry, not a canteen. That fat is why camels can skip meals for weeks.

items.prompt: Sort the cargo by its direction across the Sahara.
items.hint: Mali's lands held gold; the desert and the world beyond sent salt, scholarship, and steeds.
items.explanation: Gold, ivory, and kola nuts flowed north (kola later lent its name to cola!); salt, books, and horses came south to the Niger markets.

items.prompt: Match each name to its claim to fame.

pairs: founder-hero of the Epic of Mali
desert town with houses of salt
historian who performs the past from memory

items.hint: Two are people, two are places, one is a job.
items.explanation: Five names, one empire: its founder, its richest ruler, its city of books, its salt source, and the keepers of its story.

items.prompt: Put Mali's story in order, earliest first.

sequence: Sundiata wins the Battle of Kirina and founds the Mali Empire
Mansa Musa takes the throne of Mali
Mansa Musa's golden hajj dazzles Cairo
New mosques and schools rise in Timbuktu after the pilgrimage

items.hint: An empire must exist before its most famous emperor can rule it.
items.explanation: Founding, famous ruler, famous journey, famous city of learning — about a century of rise.

items.prompt: From Timbuktu, a caravan sets out for the salt mines of Taghaza. Which way does it head?
options: North, deep into the Sahara
South, toward the gold country
West, across the Atlantic
East, down the Niger to the sea
items.hint: Salt came from the desert.
items.explanation: The salt mines lay weeks north into the desert, while the gold lands lay south — Timbuktu thrived in between, near the bend of the Niger River.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Timbuktu — tap the lie.

truths: The Sankoré district drew scholars and thousands of students
A 1500s visitor reported that books were among the most profitable goods in Timbuktu's markets
data.lie: West Africa had no writing, so Mali's history was never written down

items.hint: What are all those famous Timbuktu manuscripts made of?
items.explanation: Hundreds of thousands of Timbuktu manuscripts — on law, astronomy, math, and poetry — survive today, many guarded by local families for centuries.

items.prompt: When Mansa Musa's caravan passed through Cairo in 1324, what happened?
items.answer: He gave away so much gold that its value in Cairo sagged for years
options: He gave away so much gold that its value in Cairo sagged for years
He bought every camel in Egypt for the journey home
Cairo's rulers refused to let him enter the city
He ran out of money and had to borrow camels
items.hint: Think supply: what happens to a treasure's value when a city is suddenly flooded with it?
items.explanation: Chroniclers wrote that gold's value in Cairo stayed low for years afterward — one traveler bent a whole economy. Many call Mansa Musa the richest person in history.

items.prompt: Mansa Musa was a devout Muslim, and his famous journey was a religious one.

lines: In 1324 he set out on the [[hajj]], the Muslim pilgrimage to the holy city of [[Mecca|Makkah]]

items.hint: The journey's name starts with h; the city is Islam's holiest.
items.explanation: His hajj crossed roughly 3,000 miles of desert — and put Mali on the map so firmly that European mapmakers later drew him holding a nugget of gold.

items.prompt: A goblin merchant filed this caravan report. Tap the claim that's wrong.

segments: Report: we left Taghaza, the mining town where walls are built from salt blocks
We marched south across the Sahara for about two months
At the Niger River markets we traded our salt for gold
The locals paid almost nothing, since salt was as common there as sand

items.hint: Remember WHY this trade existed at all.
items.explanation: Backwards! Salt was scarce and precious in the gold lands — sometimes trading weight for weight with gold. Scarcity sets the price.

items.prompt: Why zero was a revolution — a tour of the math idea you use every single day.

steps.text: Try writing 2,026 in Roman numerals: MMXXVI. Now imagine multiplying MMXXVI by XII. People wrestled with clunky systems like this for centuries.
India's idea: just TEN digits, where POSITION carries the value. In 507, the 5 means five hundreds — and the 0 bravely holds the tens place so the 5 doesn't slide over and shrink.

check.question: What job is the 0 doing in 507?
options: Holding the tens place so every digit keeps its true value
Showing that the number is even
Making the number look more impressive

steps.text: Gupta-era mathematicians went further: they treated zero as a real NUMBER you can calculate with, not just a gap. Around 628 CE, Brahmagupta wrote down its rules, like 5 − 5 = 0.
The digits traveled to Baghdad's scholars and on to Europe — which is why we call them Hindu-Arabic numerals. Every math class you've ever taken runs on this Indian invention.

check.question: Why are our digits called Hindu-Arabic numerals?
options: Born in India, they reached Europe through the Arab world
They were invented in Arabia and copied in India
European monks named them after two old books

items.prompt: Finish the captain's sailing plan for an Indian Ocean trading run.

lines: Summer: the monsoon blows from sea to land, carrying us TO India — and bringing farmers months of [[rain]]
We trade for spices, then wait for [[winter]], when the winds reverse
Riding the reversed monsoon, we sail [[home]] with full holds

items.hint: The monsoon is a schedule: in by summer, out by winter.
items.explanation: Monsoon winds made round trips predictable enough to plan years ahead — they were the engine of the whole Indian Ocean trade.

items.prompt: Which world-changing math idea came from India?
items.answer: Zero and the ten-digit place-value system
options: Zero and the ten-digit place-value system
Roman numerals
The equals sign
The multiplication table
items.hint: You used it the last time you wrote any number at all.
items.explanation: Indian mathematicians built the digits-plus-zero system the whole world now uses; it reached Europe through Arab scholars, so we call the digits Hindu-Arabic.

items.prompt: What is a monsoon?
items.answer: A seasonal wind that reverses direction during the year
options: A seasonal wind that reverses direction during the year
A sudden desert sandstorm
A giant ocean whirlpool
A week of summer thunderstorms
items.hint: It's a pattern, not a single storm.
items.explanation: Summer monsoons blow wet ocean air INTO India; winter monsoons blow dry air out to sea — a rhythm farmers and sailors both lived by.

items.prompt: Emperor Ashoka had his messages — called edicts — carved across India for everyone to read.

lines: Ashoka's edicts were carved on rocks and on tall polished stone [[pillars|pillar]]

items.hint: Some still stand today, almost 2,300 years later, topped with stone lions.
items.explanation: Ashoka's pillars rose up to 15 meters, and the four-lion carving atop one is now the national emblem of India.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about the story of zero — tap the lie.

truths: Indian mathematicians treated zero as a true number you could add and subtract
Our digits are called Hindu-Arabic numerals because they traveled from India through the Arab world
data.lie: The zero we use today was invented in ancient Rome

items.hint: Try writing zero in Roman numerals… exactly.
items.explanation: Roman numerals have no zero at all — partly why Roman arithmetic was so clumsy. Zero-as-a-number was an Indian breakthrough.

items.prompt: Match each name to its achievement.

pairs: calculated pi and said Earth spins on its axis
carved kindness laws on stone pillars
wrote the rules for calculating with zero
university that drew students from as far as China
golden age of Indian art and science

items.hint: Two mathematicians, one emperor, one school, one empire.
items.explanation: India's golden age ran on all five: rulers, scholars, schools — and brand-new math.

items.prompt: Why did Indian Ocean merchants LOVE the monsoon winds?
items.answer: The winds ran on a schedule — sail out one season, sail home the next
options: The winds ran on a schedule — sail out one season, sail home the next
The winds blew only for licensed royal ships
The winds scared pirates out of the ocean
The winds kept the sea perfectly flat
items.hint: Think of a free conveyor belt with a timetable.
items.explanation: Predictable winds meant predictable voyages: ride the summer monsoon to India, ride the winter reversal home, repeat for centuries.

items.prompt: Order the journey of India's numerals — and the empires around them — earliest first.

sequence: Emperor Ashoka raises his edict pillars across India
The Gupta golden age of art and science begins
Aryabhata, age 23, finishes his famous book of math and astronomy
Scholars in Baghdad adopt and spread the Indian numerals
Fibonacci's book introduces the digits to European merchants

items.hint: Ashoka came centuries before the Guptas; the numerals left India only after the Gupta age.
items.explanation: Roughly 250 BCE → 320 CE → 499 CE → the 800s → 1202: a great idea can take a thousand years to conquer the world.

items.prompt: Ashoka's pillar edicts and the Gupta golden age — what is the time relationship?
items.answer: Ashoka came first, more than 500 years before the Guptas
options: Ashoka came first, more than 500 years before the Guptas
The Guptas came first; Ashoka followed them
They happened in the same century, at rival courts
Historians cannot tell which came first
items.hint: Ashoka's dates are BCE; the Gupta age is CE.
items.explanation: Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire around 250 BCE; the Gupta age began around 320 CE — a gap about as long as from knights' castles to today.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about the astronomer Aryabhata — tap the lie.

truths: Aryabhata calculated pi to four decimal places: 3.1416
Aryabhata argued that the Earth spins, which is why the stars seem to wheel overhead
data.lie: Aryabhata made his discoveries using the newly invented telescope

items.hint: When was the telescope invented? (More than a thousand years after him.)
items.explanation: No telescopes existed until 1608! Aryabhata worked in 499 CE with geometry, careful sky records, and a brilliant head for numbers.

items.prompt: After the bloody Kalinga war, Emperor Ashoka famously changed. What did he do?
items.answer: Embraced Buddhist teachings and urged kindness in carved edicts
options: Embraced Buddhist teachings and urged kindness in carved edicts
Conquered three more kingdoms to celebrate the victory
Banned all religions across India
Abandoned his throne and was never seen again
items.hint: His pillars don't brag about battles — they give advice.
items.explanation: Ashoka's edicts urged mercy and respect, and he set up wells, shade trees, and medical care for people AND animals along the roads.

items.prompt: One spice from India's coasts was nicknamed 'black gold' in the ancient world.

lines: Romans paid so much gold for Indian [[pepper|black pepper]] that one Roman writer grumbled the empire's wealth was draining east

items.hint: It's still sitting next to the salt on your table.
items.explanation: Pliny the Elder complained about the cost of the spice trade; pepper was precious enough to be counted out corn by corn.

items.prompt: A rookie captain wrote this Indian Ocean trading plan. Tap the step that would sink the voyage.

segments: Plan: sail from East Africa to India for pepper and cotton, then home
Step A: leave in summer, when the monsoon blows from sea toward land, pushing us to India
Step B: trade for pepper and fine cotton cloth in the port markets
Step C: turn around immediately — the same summer wind will shove us straight home

items.hint: Can the SAME wind push you in two opposite directions?
items.explanation: You must wait for winter, when the monsoon reverses. Real captains parked in port for months — and traders built whole communities in faraway harbors while waiting.

items.prompt: Four inventions that built the modern world — let's open China's workshop.

steps.text: PAPER — perfected in Han China around 105 CE. A cheap, light writing surface meant ideas could finally travel in a sleeve instead of on heavy bamboo or costly silk.

PRINTING — Tang workshops carved whole pages into woodblocks; the Diamond Sutra of 868 CE is the world's oldest dated printed book. Around 1045, Bi Sheng invented movable type from baked clay — four centuries before Europe's first press.

check.question: Why does movable type beat carving a whole page into one block?
options: The letters can be rearranged to print ANY page
Clay blocks smell better than wood
Movable type needs no ink

steps.text: COMPASS — Song sailors steered by a magnetized needle that always finds north-south, so fleets could sail beyond sight of land even under cloudy skies.
GUNPOWDER — alchemists hunting for a life-extending elixir mixed saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal… and invented roughly the opposite. Soon China had fireworks, signal rockets, and fire arrows.

check.question: What were gunpowder's inventors actually trying to make?
options: A potion for eternal life
A louder firework
A faster kind of ink

items.prompt: Complete the story of the empire's great exam.

lines: For most of history, government jobs went to nobles' sons — by [[birth]]
Tang and Song China instead chose many officials by a days-long [[exam|test]] on the classics
Choosing people by skill instead of family is called rule by [[merit]]

items.hint: Bridge words: the opposite of 'born into the job' is earning it by…
items.explanation: Candidates sat for days in tiny exam cells, and only a small fraction passed. But the idea — jobs by merit — now runs governments around the world.

items.prompt: Three of these are among China's famous 'four great inventions.' Which one is NOT?
options: The telescope
Paper
Gunpowder
The compass
items.hint: One of these was invented in Europe in 1608.
items.explanation: The four great inventions are paper, printing, the compass, and gunpowder — the telescope came from Dutch lens-makers centuries later.

items.prompt: What was the Grand Canal built to do?
items.answer: Link northern and southern China so rice and grain could reach the capital
options: Link northern and southern China so rice and grain could reach the capital
Keep invaders away from the emperor's palace
Drain a giant swamp for farmland
Connect China to India by water
items.hint: Think of it as an 1,100-mile grocery conveyor belt.
items.explanation: The Grand Canal — still the world's longest — let southern rice feed the northern cities, and barges have used it for some 1,400 years.

items.prompt: Chinese potters fired clay so hot it turned glassy, strong, and thin.

lines: Porcelain became so famous that English speakers still call fine dishes [[china]]

items.hint: It's the country's own name, lowercase.
items.explanation: Europeans adored porcelain but couldn't reproduce it until 1708 — roughly a thousand years after Chinese kilns mastered it.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about gunpowder — tap the lie.

truths: Gunpowder was discovered by alchemists searching for a life-extending elixir
Song China used gunpowder for fireworks as well as weapons
data.lie: Gunpowder was invented in medieval Europe and later copied by China

items.hint: Follow the fireworks to their source.
items.explanation: China had gunpowder by the 800s; the recipe traveled west along trade routes and reached Europe centuries later.

items.prompt: Match each name to its claim to fame.

pairs: invented movable type from baked clay
let sailors steer beyond sight of land

items.hint: Two inventors, one admiral, two world-changing creations.
items.explanation: Paper, print, canal, compass, fleet — the toolkit of a medieval superpower.

items.prompt: What was revolutionary about China's civil-service exam?
items.answer: Government jobs could be earned by test scores, not just noble birth
options: Government jobs could be earned by test scores, not just noble birth
It was the world's first multiple-choice test
Only princes were allowed to take it
Whoever passed became the next emperor
items.hint: Who gets the job: the lord's son, or the best scorer?
items.explanation: A farmer's son who mastered the classics could become a powerful official. Candidates spent days locked in tiny exam cells — and very few passed.

items.prompt: Set China's breakthroughs in order, earliest first.

sequence: Papermaking is perfected in Han China
The Diamond Sutra becomes the world's oldest dated printed book
Bi Sheng invents movable type
Zheng He's first treasure fleet sails
The emperor's court halts the great voyages

items.hint: You need paper before you can print on it — and wealth and tech before giant fleets.
items.explanation: 105 CE → 868 → about 1045 → 1405 → 1433: invention stacked on invention until fleets of giants put to sea.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Zheng He's treasure fleet — tap the lie.

truths: Zheng He's largest ships dwarfed the ships Columbus would sail decades later
One voyage brought home a giraffe, paraded before the amazed Ming court
data.lie: The treasure voyages ended when the whole fleet was destroyed by a typhoon

items.hint: The fleet's ending was a decision, not a disaster.
items.explanation: After 1433 the court simply ORDERED the voyages stopped as too costly — the world's mightiest navy was given up by choice.

items.prompt: Why did silk and porcelain usually pass through MANY hands before reaching Europe?
items.answer: Most Silk Road merchants traveled only their own stretch, trading at oasis towns
options: Most Silk Road merchants traveled only their own stretch, trading at oasis towns
Chinese law required goods to change owners at the border
Camels could not survive more than one country's climate
Silk had to be rewoven in every city it passed
items.hint: Think relay race, not marathon.
items.explanation: The Silk Road was a chain of middlemen, each adding a markup — one big reason Europeans later went hunting for a sea route to Asia.

items.prompt: In 1900, a sealed cave near Dunhuang revealed a scroll dated 868 CE — a world record holder.

lines: The Diamond Sutra is the world's oldest dated [[printed]] book

items.hint: Not written by hand — stamped from carved woodblocks.
items.explanation: A whole scroll printed almost 600 years before Gutenberg — and its final line says it was made 'for universal free distribution.'

items.prompt: Sort the Silk Road traffic: which direction did each mostly travel in this era?
items.hint: China exported its crafts; horses, glass, and new religions rode in.
items.explanation: Silk, porcelain, and eventually the secret of papermaking flowed west; horses, glass, and Buddhism flowed east. Trade routes carry ideas, not just goods.

items.prompt: A museum placard about the treasure fleet has one error. Tap it.

segments: Seven expeditions visited Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa
The flagship made Columbus's Santa María look like a lifeboat
The voyages were so profitable that China never stopped exploring

items.hint: How did the treasure-fleet story actually end?
items.explanation: The court ended the voyages by decree in 1433 and turned inward — one of history's great what-ifs, just 59 years before Columbus sailed.

items.prompt: Feudalism: the chain of promises that organized a continent without salaries.

steps.text: Start at the top: the king claims all the land but cannot farm or guard it alone. So he grants huge chunks to lords — in exchange for loyalty and soldiers whenever war comes.
Lords pass it on: they grant smaller pieces to knights, their vassals. The knight's side of the deal: fight for the lord, often for a set number of days each year.

check.question: What did a vassal owe in exchange for land?
options: Loyalty and military service
A monthly payment in gold
Nothing — the land was a free gift

steps.text: At the base: serfs. They farm the lord's fields and hand over part of every harvest; in return they get protection and land to live on. Bound to the manor, they need permission to leave — yet unlike enslaved people, they cannot be sold away from their land.
So feudalism is a pyramid of deals: land flows down, loyalty and work flow up. Hardly any money changes hands — land IS the money.

check.question: In the feudal pyramid, what flows DOWN?
options: Land and protection
Harvests and labor
Loyalty and service

items.prompt: A siege approaches! Complete the castle's defense rundown.

lines: First obstacle: the ring of water called the [[moat]]
The gatehouse lifts the [[drawbridge]] so no one can cross
Down crashes the iron grate — the [[portcullis]]

items.hint: All three words were on the castle-blueprint screen.
items.explanation: Moat, drawbridge, portcullis — three layers before anyone touches the walls. Defenders could even drop stones through 'murder holes' in the gate ceiling.

items.prompt: What did a serf give the lord of the manor in exchange for protection and land to farm?
items.answer: Labor and a share of the harvest
options: Labor and a share of the harvest
Gold coins every month
Nothing — serfs were paid wages
Knights for the lord's army
items.hint: Serfs had almost no money — so what could they pay with?
items.explanation: Serfs paid in work and crops — they even paid fees to grind grain at the lord's mill. It wasn't slavery, but it was far from freedom.

items.prompt: Castle windows were often just narrow slits in the thick walls. Why?
items.answer: Archers inside could shoot out while staying nearly impossible to hit
options: Archers inside could shoot out while staying nearly impossible to hit
Glass was too expensive for any castle
Narrow windows were purely decorative
They kept the castle cooler in summer
items.hint: Imagine trying to aim INTO a slit from 100 meters away.
items.explanation: Arrow slits gave every defender a wide view and a tiny silhouette — castle design is geometry with attitude.

items.prompt: Guilds gave us a word you still use for any great work of art.

lines: To rise from apprentice to master, a craftsman presented his finest work — literally his [[masterpiece]]

items.hint: Master + piece.
items.explanation: Your master-piece proved you could join the masters. Bonus etymology: 'journeyman' comes from the French journée, because he was paid by the DAY.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about serfs — tap the lie.

truths: Serfs owed the lord labor and part of their harvest in exchange for protection
Unlike enslaved people, serfs could not be bought and sold away from their land
data.lie: Serfs were free to pack up and move to another village whenever they wished

items.hint: The word 'bound' is the key to serfdom.
items.explanation: Serfs were tied to the manor — leaving required the lord's permission. (After the plague, though, scarce workers found they could finally bargain.)

items.prompt: Match each medieval feature to its job.

pairs: iron grate that seals the gate
the strongest tower — the last refuge
outside prop that lets cathedral walls soar
stone monster that is secretly a rain spout

items.hint: Three guard a castle, two belong to cathedrals.
items.explanation: Even the monsters had day jobs: gargoyles spit rainwater clear of the walls so it wouldn't gnaw the stone.

items.prompt: Whose duty is it? Sort each duty to its feudal role.

Lord: grants land in exchange for loyalty
Knight: fights on horseback for his lord
Serf: farms the fields and owes part of the harvest
cannot leave the manor without permission

items.hint: Land-giver, land-defender, land-worker.
items.explanation: Lord, knight, serf — the whole system ran on land and loyalty instead of salaries.

items.prompt: Order the steps of a guild career, from a young baker's first day to owning the shop.

sequence: Join a master's household as a young apprentice
Spend about seven years learning the craft for room and board
Work as a journeyman, earning pay by the day
Present a masterpiece for the guild's judgment
Be accepted as a master and open your own shop

items.hint: Learn free, then earn daily, then prove yourself.
items.explanation: Apprentice → journeyman → master: the guild ladder controlled quality in every trade, from bread to goldwork.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about the Black Death — tap the lie.

truths: The plague reached Europe on trading ships and spread along trade routes
So many workers died that survivors could demand better pay and freedoms
data.lie: Medieval doctors quickly identified the germ and cured the plague

items.hint: Germs weren't discovered for another 500 years.
items.explanation: No one knew bacteria existed — physicians blamed 'bad air.' The disease killed perhaps a third of Europe in about four years.

items.prompt: Why were books so rare and precious in medieval Europe?
items.answer: Each copy was handwritten — one book could take a scribe a year
options: Each copy was handwritten — one book could take a scribe a year
Paper had not been invented anywhere in the world yet
Reading was illegal outside the monasteries
Most books were burned every winter for heat
items.hint: Think about how a copy got made before machines.
items.explanation: Monks copied texts letter by letter in the scriptorium, decorating pages with real gold — that's why it's called 'illumination.' (And paper DID exist — China had it for a thousand years.)

items.prompt: After the Black Death, why could surviving peasants suddenly demand wages and freedoms?
items.answer: Workers were scarce, so their labor was worth far more
options: Workers were scarce, so their labor was worth far more
The king ordered every lord to pay equal wages
Peasants had inherited the lords' castles
Food had become free for everyone
items.hint: Supply and demand — but for workers.
items.explanation: With perhaps a third of Europe gone, lords competed for field hands; many serfs bargained for pay or left for the towns. Catastrophe cracked feudalism.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about medieval minds — tap the lie.

truths: Medieval university students studied astronomy as a core subject
Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was a sphere
data.lie: People in the Middle Ages believed the Earth was flat

items.hint: This 'fact' about the past is itself the myth.
items.explanation: Scholars had known Earth's shape since the ancient Greeks; the 'medieval flat-earthers' story was largely spread by a novelist's Columbus tale in the 1800s.

items.prompt: Legendary: It's 1351. Half the village fields stand empty, and a neighboring lord is offering real wages for harvest help. As the manor's lord, what should you EXPECT?
items.answer: Serfs gain bargaining power — some will demand pay or slip away to better offers
options: Serfs gain bargaining power — some will demand pay or slip away to better offers
Serfs will work double for free out of gratitude
Wages everywhere will fall because food is scarce
Nothing changes, since serfs may never leave a manor
items.hint: Scarce workers + competing employers = ?
items.explanation: Exactly what happened: wages rose, old labor duties crumbled, and within a few generations serfdom faded across much of Western Europe.

items.prompt: The press that made ideas go viral — let's see how Gutenberg's machine worked its magic.

steps.text: Before 1440: every European book was copied by hand. A Bible took a scribe about a year, so books cost a fortune and most people never owned a single one.

Gutenberg's combo, around 1440: metal MOVABLE TYPE (cast letters you rearrange endlessly), a screw press borrowed from wine-making, and oily ink that stuck to metal. Set a page once — print hundreds of copies.

check.question: What made movable type such a time-saver?
options: Letters could be reused and rearranged for any page
The letters were prettier than handwriting
Each page was carved fresh from one wood block

steps.text: The math is wild: a press team could pull hundreds of pages a DAY. By 1500 — barely 50 years later — European presses had printed millions of books.
Cheap books meant more people learned to read, scientists could compare notes across countries, and new ideas could not be hushed up. Printing didn't just copy the Renaissance — it spread it.

check.question: Why did printing speed up science?
options: Discoveries could be shared widely and checked by others
Printers performed the experiments themselves
Printed books made telescopes cheaper

items.prompt: Finish Galileo's evidence chain like a scientist.

lines: Claim: not everything in the sky circles the Earth
Evidence: night after night in 1610, Galileo watched four moons circling [[Jupiter]]
Reasoning: if moons orbit another planet, Earth is not the center of every orbit
Backing claims with [[evidence]] became the habit we now call science

items.hint: Bridge flashback: which planet did he aim at, and what must back up a claim?
items.explanation: He even named the moons the 'Medicean stars' after the Medici, his hoped-for patrons — flattery and data in a single discovery.

items.prompt: What changed about books after Gutenberg's press, around 1440?
items.answer: From rare, costly, hand-copied treasures to printed and affordable
options: From rare, costly, hand-copied treasures to printed and affordable
They became smaller but stayed just as rare
They could finally include pictures
Nothing — monks copied faster than the machines
items.hint: Think speed of copying.
items.explanation: Within 50 years, presses had printed millions of volumes — more books than Europe's scribes had managed in centuries.

items.prompt: The Medici of Florence were famous as patrons. A patron is…
items.answer: A wealthy supporter who pays for artists' and scientists' work
options: A wealthy supporter who pays for artists' and scientists' work
A guard who protects famous paintings
A judge in painting competitions
A merchant who sells brushes and paint
items.hint: Bridge vocab — think 'support.'
items.explanation: Medici banking money backed Botticelli and a teenage Michelangelo; Galileo even named Jupiter's moons after the family to win their support.

items.prompt: Leonardo da Vinci, a left-hander, filled thousands of notebook pages writing right to left.

lines: His reversed script is called [[mirror]] writing

items.hint: You'd need a piece of bathroom equipment to read it easily.
items.explanation: Hold a page up to a mirror and it reads normally. No one is sure why he did it — smudge-free lefty writing is one good guess.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Gutenberg — tap the lie.

truths: Gutenberg's press in Mainz was printing by around 1440
By 1500, European presses had printed millions of books
data.lie: Gutenberg was the first person in the world to print a book

items.hint: Think back to a certain 868 CE scroll from China…
items.explanation: China printed the Diamond Sutra six centuries earlier, and Bi Sheng made movable type around 1045. Gutenberg's breakthrough was a metal-type press system that fit alphabets perfectly.

items.prompt: Match each Renaissance name to its claim to fame.

pairs: notebooks crammed with inventions and anatomy
book putting the Sun at the center
telescope evidence for the new astronomy

items.hint: One printer, one artist-engineer, one family of bankers, two sky-watchers.
items.explanation: Press, patrons, paintings, planets — the Renaissance toolkit in five names.

items.prompt: Around 1413, Brunelleschi showed painters a trick called linear perspective. What does it do?
items.answer: Makes a flat painting look deep, with lines meeting at a vanishing point
options: Makes a flat painting look deep, with lines meeting at a vanishing point
Makes paint dry faster in cold weather
Lets painters mix any color from three pigments
Shrinks a portrait down to coin size
items.hint: Picture train tracks: what do the rails seem to do far away?
items.explanation: Parallel lines drawn toward one vanishing point trick the eye into seeing depth — suddenly paintings looked like windows you could step through.

items.prompt: Order the road from hand-copied books to telescope-tested skies.

sequence: Monks copy each book by hand, one slow page at a time
Gutenberg's movable-type press starts printing in Mainz
Printed books spread across Europe by the millions
Copernicus publishes his Sun-centered model
Galileo publishes what his telescope revealed

items.hint: Copying → printing → spreading → big claim → telescope evidence.
items.explanation: The 1440s → by 1500 → 1543 → 1610: each step armed the next. Print carried Copernicus and Galileo to every corner of Europe.

items.prompt: Grand timeline! Order these five moments from your whole journey, earliest first.

sequence: Sundiata founds the Mali Empire
Mansa Musa's golden hajj dazzles Cairo
Gutenberg's press prints its first pages
Columbus crosses the Atlantic
Galileo aims his telescope at Jupiter

items.hint: Mali's story is the 1200s–1300s; print is the mid-1400s; the telescope is the newest of all.
items.explanation: About 1235 → 1324 → the 1440s → 1492 → 1610: four centuries from the Lion King of Mali to moons around Jupiter.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Galileo — tap the lie.

truths: Galileo improved a Dutch spyglass design until it magnified about 20 times
Galileo discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter

items.hint: Whose patent application reached the Dutch government in 1608?
items.explanation: Dutch spectacle-makers built the first telescopes; Galileo's genius was supercharging one, aiming it at the SKY, and publishing the evidence.

items.prompt: A friend insists: 'Heavy objects obviously fall faster — the ancient books say so.' What is the Scientific Revolution's reply?
items.answer: Test it and watch — evidence outranks old books
options: Test it and watch — evidence outranks old books
Older books are always right
Take a vote among the smartest people
Whoever argues loudest wins
items.hint: Claim, evidence, reasoning — what's missing from 'books say so'?
items.explanation: Galileo reportedly tested falling weights and showed they land together. The new habit — observe, don't just trust authority — is the same CER you use in science class.

items.prompt: Leonardo refused to pick just one job.

lines: He was equal parts artist and [[engineer]]: between portraits he sketched flying machines, gears, and anatomy

items.hint: Someone who designs machines.
items.explanation: About 7,000 notebook pages survive — studies of bird wings, water, war machines, even a robot knight. The ultimate 'why not both?'

items.prompt: A museum placard about the new astronomy has one error. Tap it.

segments: In 1543, Copernicus published a model with the Sun, not Earth, at the center
In 1610, Galileo's telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter
Galileo's discoveries spread slowly, because each copy of his book had to be hand-copied by monks

items.hint: What machine had already existed for 170 years by 1610?
items.explanation: Printing presses had been running since the 1440s — Galileo's 'Starry Messenger' sold out almost immediately. Print is HOW the new astronomy went viral.

items.prompt: The explorer's toolkit — mostly borrowed! Let's see what made ocean crossings possible.

steps.text: The motive: spices. A small sack of pepper or nutmeg could repay a whole voyage — IF you could buy it at the source instead of through a dozen middlemen, each one charging a markup.
The ship: the caravel — small and quick, with triangular lateen sails that let it zigzag INTO the wind instead of waiting for a perfect breeze. Columbus's Niña and Pinta were caravels.

check.question: What superpower did lateen sails give a caravel?
options: Sailing at an angle into the wind
Sailing twice as fast downwind
Sailing with half the crew asleep

steps.text: The tools — imported: the compass came from China, and the astrolabe was perfected by astronomers of the Islamic world. Measure the noon sun's height and you know your latitude — how far north or south you've sailed.
So the Age of Exploration was a global team effort before it even began: Chinese needles, Arab star-math, Portuguese hulls — and a planet about to be stitched together.

check.question: Which is TRUE about the explorers' toolkit?
options: Key tools were invented elsewhere and adopted by Europeans
Europeans invented the compass and astrolabe from scratch
Explorers navigated by pure guesswork

items.prompt: Complete the Columbian Exchange ledger.

lines: Sailing east to Europe: corn, tomatoes, and [[potatoes]]
Sailing west to the Americas: wheat, cattle, and [[horses]]
Crossing invisibly with the crews: deadly [[germs|diseases]], like smallpox

items.hint: The bridge named all three: Ireland's future crop, the Plains' future rides, and the invisible passengers.
items.explanation: Foods enriched menus on both sides of the ocean, but the germs were catastrophic: Indigenous peoples had no immunity, and epidemics swept the Americas.

items.prompt: An Italian chef in the year 1400 could NOT have cooked with which ingredient?
options: Tomatoes
Olive oil
Wheat flour
Garlic
items.hint: One of these is a New World native.
items.explanation: Tomatoes are American plants — Italy only met them after the Columbian Exchange. Pizza as we know it is younger than the telescope!

items.prompt: Why did explorers prize the caravel?
items.answer: Its triangular sails let it sail at an angle into the wind
options: Its triangular sails let it sail at an angle into the wind
It was the biggest ship ever built
Its hull was plated with iron
It could sail itself while the crew slept
items.hint: Think about sailing TOWARD where the wind comes from.
items.explanation: Lateen sails meant no more waiting for a perfect breeze. Bonus: ships usually carried cats to guard the food stores from rats.

items.prompt: The needle that pointed the explorers' way was not a European invention.

lines: The magnetic compass was invented in [[China]]

items.hint: Zheng He's sailors steered by it decades before Columbus was born.
items.explanation: The compass reached Europe through Indian Ocean and Mediterranean trade — the Age of Exploration ran on borrowed brilliance.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Columbus's 1492 voyage — tap the lie.

truths: Educated Europeans in 1492 already knew the Earth was round — the debate was about its size
Columbus believed he had reached islands near Asia, so he called the people 'Indians'
data.lie: Columbus's crew feared they would sail off the edge of a flat Earth

items.hint: You busted this same myth back in Medieval Europe.
items.explanation: The real argument: scholars said the globe was far bigger than Columbus claimed — and they were RIGHT. An unexpected continent is what saved his fleet from starving mid-ocean.

items.prompt: Match each piece of the explorer's world to its description.

pairs: China's gift: a needle that finds north
measures a star's height to find latitude
small cargo worth a fortune in Europe
first ship to sail all the way around the world

items.hint: Two tools, one ship type, one cargo, one record-setter.
items.explanation: With borrowed tools and new hulls, a single returning spice ship could make its investors rich.

items.prompt: Historians sum up the explorers' motives as three G's.

lines: The three G's: [[gold]], glory, and God

items.hint: The first G is a precious metal.
items.explanation: Wealth, fame, and spreading their faith drove the voyages — and spices were the fastest wealth of all.

items.prompt: Order the age of ocean voyages, earliest first.

sequence: Zheng He's treasure fleets cross the Indian Ocean
Dias rounds Africa's southern tip
Columbus reaches the Caribbean
Da Gama sails all the way to India
Magellan's expedition finishes circling the globe

items.hint: China's fleets came first; the Spanish circle closed last, in 1522.
items.explanation: 1405–1433 → 1488 → 1492 → 1498 → 1522: within one long century, the oceans became highways.

items.prompt: Columbian Exchange sort: which side of the ocean did each come from FIRST?
items.hint: Ask: could a medieval European knight have eaten it? Then it's Old World.
items.explanation: No chocolate in all of Europe, no horses in all the Americas — 1492 rewired every menu on Earth.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about Magellan's expedition — tap the lie.

truths: The expedition left Spain with five ships and about 270 men
Only one ship, the Victoria, made it home, carrying 18 exhausted sailors
data.lie: Magellan himself completed the first voyage around the world

items.hint: Check what happened in the Philippines in 1521.
items.explanation: Magellan was killed mid-voyage in the Philippines; Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522. The EXPEDITION circled the globe — its commander did not.

items.prompt: Why were European diseases like smallpox so catastrophic in the Americas?
items.answer: Indigenous peoples had never met these germs, so they had no immunity
options: Indigenous peoples had never met these germs, so they had no immunity
The American climate made every disease stronger
Cures existed in Europe but were left behind
The diseases spread through gold and silver
items.hint: Bridge vocab: immunity.
items.explanation: Epidemics raced ahead of the explorers themselves, killing most of the population in many regions — the deadliest consequence of the Exchange.

items.prompt: Which statement about the American colonies' sugar plantations is historically accurate?
items.answer: They ran on the forced labor of enslaved African people, shipped across the Atlantic
options: They ran on the forced labor of enslaved African people, shipped across the Atlantic
They paid high wages to volunteer workers from Europe
They were worked mainly by Spanish nobles
Sugar grew wild there and needed almost no workers
items.hint: This is the era's hardest truth — face it squarely.
items.explanation: The Atlantic slave trade forcibly transported more than 12 million Africans over its centuries. Honest history counts the era's costs as well as its discoveries.

items.prompt: Legendary: In 1504, a Venetian pepper merchant finds his prices undercut and his usual suppliers nearly empty-handed. What best explains his crisis?
items.answer: Portuguese ships now sail directly to India, skipping the middlemen Venice relied on
options: Portuguese ships now sail directly to India, skipping the middlemen Venice relied on
Europeans suddenly stopped eating pepper
Pepper had begun growing wild across northern Italy
Venice's ships had all been lost in a storm
items.hint: Follow da Gama's 1498 route — and think about markups.
items.explanation: Da Gama's sea route let Portugal buy pepper at the source, bypassing the old relay of middlemen Venice depended on. One new route rocked whole economies.
